title: How To Have Behavior-Changing Influence With Students with-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: This article translates the Law of Reciprocity — the idea that going out of your way to please someone makes them want to please you back — into concrete daily practice. Linsin's list includes a genuinely no-strings-attached personal hello, being consistently pleasant so rapport develops without effort, actively caring for students in word and action, and rigorously following through on every stated consequence without judgment. He emphasizes that consistent enforcement paired with pleasantness is what gives a teacher real leverage over classroom behavior, and that staying calm rather than visibly stressed protects that influence. The piece closes with a warning that this influence can't be turned on and off — it must be sustained as a genuine persona, since even occasional slip-ups can significantly weaken its power.
points: A genuine, no-strings-attached personal greeting is offered as an easy, powerful entry point into the Law of Reciprocity.
Being consistently pleasant throughout the school day is described as making rapport come to the teacher effortlessly.
Following through on every stated consequence — without lecturing or judgment — builds the trust that anchors real influence.
Staying visibly calm rather than showing stress or frustration is necessary to preserve the teacher's influence over students.
The influence built through this approach must be sustained consistently, since even a few slip-ups can significantly weaken it.
quotes: The Law of Reciprocity says that when you go out of your way to please someone, they’ll want to please you right back. It’s a deep-seated psychological urge that is nearly impossible to resist.
Make your gesture with no strings attached. It’s so simple, yet so powerful. This alone can do wonders.
If you can be consistently pleasant throughout every school day, you have the keys to the kingdom. Rapport will come effortlessly because students will come to you instead of the other way around.
You must, must, must do what you say you’ll do. Few teachers fall into this special category. But if you do, if you can be a person of your word, truly, it changes everything.

You must enforce consequences consistently and be pleasant at the same time . Once you’re able to do this by course of habit, you’ll experience a level of power and leverage over classroom behavior you never thought possible.
You can’t just try it out for a day or two. You can’t fall on and off the horse. The power grows stronger with time and the longer you maintain your new persona.
